newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel expects no pressure from re-elected Clinton.
newsitem.headline: Israel expects no pressure from re-elected Clinton.

text.p: Israel told the Arabs on Wednesday not to expect re-elected U.S. President Bill Clinton to pressure Israel into making peace concessions.
"The date of the American elections does not materially change their (Arabs') need and their responsibility to enter negotiations," Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said.
"No one will do the job for them," he told reporters.

Some Arabs and Israelis expect that a second-term Clinton, eyeing his place in history rather than another election, will lean on Netanyahu to carry out peace deals the Israeli right-winger reluctantly inherited when he took office in June.
On Tuesday, Netanyahu said he would not be "whipped" by the next president into making compromises and Palestinian President Yasser Arafat was wrong to think so.
"If he is waiting for the great pressure that has to come from Washington, he will be disappointed because it will not come," the Israeli leader said.
In the West Bank on Wednesday, Arafat hailed Clinton's victory, saying it would give a push to Middle East peace.
Palestinian peace negotiator Hassan Asfour said he hoped Clinton would press Israel to implement a long-overdue troop redeployment in the West Bank town of Hebron.
But U.S. Consul General Edward Abington said there were as yet no plans for Clinton's Middle East envoy Dennis Ross to return to the region to try to broker a deal.

Clinton has played a key role in Israeli-PLO peace moves, most recently calling Netanyahu and Arafat to an emergency White House summit in October to halt gunbattles and clashes unprecedented in three years of peacemaking.

The U.S. president all but openly endorsed former prime minister Shimon Peres over Netanyahu for Israel's May 29 election. A Nobel peace laureate, Peres favours a U.S.-backed land-for-peace policy opposed by Netanyahu.
"Bill Clinton is a true friend of Israel and the Jewish people," Netanyahu said, adding he expected the "new-old administration" to help Israel and the Arabs pursue peace.
Opposition leader Peres, in rare agreement with Netanyahu, told army radio: "I do not foresee pressure from the United States."
Israeli analysts say the first indication of any shift in U.S. policy will be in Clinton's appointment of a secretary of state to replace Warren Christopher, widely expected to retire.

Clinton's repeated commitment to Israel's security has many doubting he will use the tremendous leverage he might have over it. Israel, at $3 billion a year, receives more U.S. aid than any other country.
In his four years at the White House, Clinton has hosted three Arab-Israeli summits, visited Israel twice and sent Christopher to the Middle East more than 20 times -- compared with once to Beijing.

Opinion polls last week showed Israelis would overwhelmingly have backed Clinton over Republican Bob Dole. Clinton would have won 85 to 87 percent of the "Israeli" vote compared with only about half the popular U.S. vote.
U.S.-sponsored Israeli-PLO talks are deadlocked over implementation of the troop pullback in Hebron where 400 Jews live and study among 100,000 Palestinians.

Palestinians accuse Israel of trying to renegotiate the Hebron deal signed by the centre-left government that Netanyahu ousted. The redeployment, due in March, was delayed by a wave of Islamic militant attacks in Israel.
Netanyahu says he wants to modify the deal to better safeguard the Jews in Hebron.
